clue.text: My jape is silly, overshadowing isolated overnight events

indicators.note: something silly is muddled and nonsensical, so these letters lose their sensible order
to overshadow is to loom over and cover, so one piece spreads over and around another

blocks.note: eight letters taken as written for rearranging
something isolated stands apart from the rest

explanation.surface: Someone admits their prank was daft, and it rather spoiled some lonely all-night happenings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Isolated' reads as describing the events, but it is wordplay for a word meaning separate, which sits inside the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepovers where guests come in nightwear and stay till morning are gatherings that run through the night.

clue.text: 'Table' in France: a single dish with water

blocks.note: plat is the French word for a dish or course
eau is French for water

explanation.surface: A note on French dining: the word for a table, then one course served with water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like it governs only 'Table', but it tells you both pieces are French words; the English answer happens to be built from them.
explanation.definitionFit: A tableland is a raised area of flat ground, and geographers use 'table' as a synonym for such elevated level country.

clue.text: Writer in bliss before seeing cheque ... gutted

indicators.note: a gutted thing has had its insides removed, leaving only the outside shell
placing one piece before the next sets them in reading order

blocks.note: bliss is great joy
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: An author in raptures, until the payment arrives and turns out to be disappointing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gutted' reads as British slang for bitterly disappointed, but it means the middle of the word is removed. JOY plus CE gives JOYCE.
explanation.definitionFit: James Joyce, the Irish novelist behind Ulysses, is a famous author, so the surname fits a general word for a literary figure.

clue.text: Troll using some 'gammon' stereotypes

indicators.note: using only some of the text means a run of letters is lifted from inside it

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: An online provocateur leans on lazy labels like 'gammon' to bait people.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sense of troll is the internet provocateur; the definition is the folk-tale creature. 'Gammon' is British slang for a red-faced reactionary older man.
explanation.definitionFit: Trolls in Scandinavian folklore are ugly cave-dwelling giants, a kind of fearsome mythical creature.

clue.text: Correspondence from overseas resort captured Tropics

indicators.note: read as re-sort, it asks for the letters to be sorted into a fresh order

blocks.note: fifteen letters taken as written for rearranging

explanation.surface: A note sent home from a holiday spot that caught the warmth of the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' sits naturally as a holiday destination, but it is re-sort, the anagram signal for the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A card with a photograph on the front is the classic message holidaymakers mail home from abroad.

clue.text: Equality – with prince becoming king – it's seldom seen

definitions.note: a clause describing the answer, which is a noun

indicators.note: one thing becoming another means a letter is swapped for a different one

blocks.note: parity is equality of status or value
P is a standard abbreviation for prince
R stands for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A wry political aside: true equality, with a monarch in charge, is something you hardly ever witness.
explanation.walkthrough: PARITY loses its P and takes an R in its place, giving RARITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uncommon that people only occasionally encounter is a rarity, so the clause describes the noun.

clue.text: Ordinarily, flipping Luxembourg and Austria mostly backslide, 'neutral; independent'

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
flipping something over turns it the other way round

blocks.note: L is the international vehicle code for Luxembourg
A is the international vehicle code for Austria
to renege is to go back on a promise
N is the standard abbreviation for neutral
I is the standard abbreviation for independent

explanation.surface: Two small European nations are said to drift from their neutral, independent stance as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive, but it reverses the string L A RENEG N I, built from car codes, RENEGE without its last E, and two abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean usually or as a rule, describing what happens in most cases.

clue.text: They rebuke people found on roofs

blocks.note: first meaning: those who slate, that is criticise harshly
second meaning: tradesmen who lay roof tiles of a particular stone

explanation.walkthrough: To slate is British for criticising severely, as in a newspaper review; the same word names those who cover roofs with slate.
explanation.definitionFit: Harsh critics and roofing tradesmen share one agent noun, formed from two different senses of the verb.

clue.text: Bootlegging, excluding number that's suggestive

indicators.note: excluding something leaves it out, so those letters are removed

blocks.note: illegal copying or smuggling of goods is piracy
pi is the famous mathematical constant

explanation.surface: Smuggled goods, minus one particular item, turn out to be a bit saucy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' wants to be a song or a count; it is the constant PI, removed from the front of PIRACY.
explanation.definitionFit: Risqué material that hints at sex is described as mildly indecent, an everyday synonym.

clue.text: A nun, woozy with a cigar from somewhere in Central America

indicators.note: a woozy head is dizzy and confused, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sister of the convent, light-headed after puffing on a cigar from that region.
explanation.walkthrough: The cigar suggests Cuba, but Cuba is in the Caribbean; the definition asks for an adjective from a mainland country, which also makes cigars.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicaragua is a country on the Central American isthmus, so the adjective names its people and products.

clue.text: Small amount of money Everyman's hiding, getting stick

indicators.note: something hiding another keeps it tucked away inside

blocks.note: a cent is a hundredth of a dollar or euro
the setter refers to themself, so Everyman is me

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to squirrelling away a few coins and being told off for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting stick' reads as being criticised; here stick is a verb, the definition. The 's in Everyman's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To cement things is to bind them firmly together, so the verb is a synonym of attach or glue.

clue.text: Without a plan to lose home, becoming derelict

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, leaving the rest

blocks.note: something not planned was not meant
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: Someone drifting with no plan loses the roof over their head and falls into ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: IN for 'at home' is a crossword staple; take it out of UNINTENDED to leave UNTENDED.
explanation.definitionFit: A building nobody looks after falls into neglect, so abandoned and uncared-for are close synonyms.

clue.text: Dame; unsettling macabre author, uncomfortable reading including eerie Rebecca, primarily!

definitions.text: Dame; unsettling macabre author, uncomfortable reading including eerie Rebecca

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: Dame; unsettling macabre author, uncomfortable reading including eerie Rebecca
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the nine words

explanation.surface: A description of a titled woman writer whose dark, uneasy novels include the chilling Rebecca.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: its initials spell the name, and read straight it describes her.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Daphne du Maurier wrote the gothic novel Rebecca and macabre tales such as The Birds and Don't Look Now.

clue.text: Topple after a little Negroni and fizz as starters

indicators.note: only a little of the word is used, namely its first letter
one piece placed after another sets the reading order

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the cocktail
to tip over is to topple
Asti is a sparkling Italian wine

explanation.surface: Falling over after a dash of Negroni and some bubbly to begin the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The Italian theme of Negroni and fizz points the right way: the answer is the Italian plural for first courses.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipasti are Italian appetisers served before the main meal, so they are the opening courses.

clue.text: Some Blairism that's essential in vision

indicators.note: only some of the word is wanted, a run of letters from inside it

blocks.note: the run of letters inside the political label

explanation.surface: A remark that part of Tony Blair's politics was crucial to his big-picture outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Vision suggests political vision; the definition means eyesight.
explanation.definitionFit: The coloured ring of the eye controls how much light enters the pupil, so it is a vital part of sight.

clue.text: Tasteless rubbish! American! I'm off!

blocks.note: tat is cheap, tasteless junk
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Someone storms out after denouncing vulgar American trash.
explanation.walkthrough: Tat is British for cheap, gaudy goods; ta-ta is a casual British goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: Announcing one's departure is a way of saying goodbye, and this informal farewell does exactly that.

clue.text: Pour most of the whiskey out – what you may do later?

definitions.note: a clause describing the answer, a verb phrase

indicators.note: most of means all but a bit, so the last letter goes
out can mean disordered or wrong, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
the word with its last letter removed
whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Tip away most of that liquor, or you may regret it in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of the whiskey' seems to be one phrase, but 'most of' works only on 'the', and whiskey is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sick is a likely consequence of drinking too much, so the clue hints at vomiting after a heavy session.

clue.text: Monsieur altered canton to include limits of Basel and an Alp

indicators.note: the limits of a thing are its edges, so its first and last letters
something altered has been changed, so the letters are rearranged
including means taking in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: M. is the French abbreviation for monsieur
taken as written
the first and last letters of the Swiss city

explanation.surface: A Frenchman redraws a Swiss district's boundary so that it takes in the edges of Basel and a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all Swiss: a canton is one of Switzerland's states. Monsieur is abbreviated M. in French, as Mr is in English.
explanation.definitionFit: Mont Blanc is the highest peak in the Alps, on the French-Italian border, so it is one of those mountains.

clue.text: Also, the German harbours run as per specifications

indicators.note: to harbour is to shelter, so one piece is kept inside another

blocks.note: too means also
der is the German masculine word for 'the'
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A German, too, runs a port according to the rule book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbours' looks like a noun about ports, but it is a verb: the two words for 'also' and 'the German' together hold the letter for run.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods made to order are produced exactly following the customer's stated requirements, as the phrase means.

clue.text: Time to note: what was more savoury now more indecent

indicators.note: one letter going to another marks a swap of one for the other

blocks.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
N is short for note
food with more flavour is more delicious

explanation.surface: A diarist records that something once more appetising has turned rather more smutty.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the T of TASTIER to N and the word flips from delicious to unpleasant; savoury also hints at unsavoury.
explanation.definitionFit: Nasty can mean obscene or offensive, so the comparative is a synonym for being more lewd.

clue.text: Tea, followed by tea dance

indicators.note: one thing followed by another puts them side by side in order

blocks.note: cha is British slang for tea
the same slang word again

explanation.surface: An afternoon programme: a cuppa, then a tea dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea dance' looks like one phrase, an old-fashioned afternoon social; split it, and dance is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The cha-cha is a lively Latin American ballroom dance of Cuban origin.

clue.text: Scratching head, orthopod's performing skilful manœuvre

indicators.note: to scratch is to strike out, and the head is the front, so the opening letter goes
performing suggests putting on an act, so the letters move into new positions

blocks.note: the bone surgeon's possessive form minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A puzzled bone surgeon pulls off a deft operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scratching head' suggests puzzlement; it means delete the first letter. An orthopod is slang for an orthopaedic surgeon.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis or badminton this delicate stroke barely clears the net, a deft piece of play.

clue.text: Haunt with unnatural sobs describing evacuated entrails

indicators.note: unnatural means not in the normal state, so the letters are rearranged
evacuated means emptied, leaving only the outer letters
to describe a circle is to draw round, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A gothic ghost tormenting someone with eerie sobs while talking of disembowelled innards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' is the geometry sense, to draw around, not to give an account.
explanation.definitionFit: A thought that haunts you preoccupies your mind constantly, which is what to obsess means.

clue.text: Hone temper

blocks.note: first meaning: to sharpen a razor on a leather strap
second meaning: a sulk or fit of bad mood, in British slang

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like metalworking verbs, hone and temper steel; only the first is, and the second is the British noun for a bad mood.
explanation.definitionFit: A barber sharpens a razor on a leather strap, and a sulky outburst is called being in a mood of that name.

clue.text: Leafy green – or cheese and white wine? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means without one half, so only part of the word is kept

blocks.note: Swiss cheese is the holey kind such as Emmental
a popular white grape and wine

explanation.surface: A host weighing up salad against a cheese board with white wine, and the guest replies emphatically yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely!', but here it keeps the first half of CHARDONNAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Swiss chard is a beet grown for its large edible leaves, a vegetable cooked like spinach.

clue.text: Complain as storyteller returning

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so it runs backwards

blocks.note: a liar tells stories that are untrue

explanation.surface: Grumbling as the narrator comes back.
explanation.walkthrough: A storyteller is a teller of tales in the sense of fibs, giving LIAR.
explanation.definitionFit: To rail against something is to protest bitterly about it, a stronger synonym for grumbling.

clue.text: Strict type of ballerina, initially narcissistic drama queen withholding support

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives its opening letter
split as with plus holding, it attaches one piece alongside another

blocks.note: a prima ballerina is the leading dancer of a company
the opening letters of the two words
a prop holds something up
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher

explanation.surface: A portrait of a strait-laced star dancer, self-obsessed and theatrical, refusing to lend a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drama queen' looks like one phrase, but drama supplies only its initial and queen is the royal cipher. 'Withholding' must be read loosely as 'with holding', since the queen follows the support rather than surrounding it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone stiffly correct and formal in manners, keen on rules, is described with this idiomatic phrase.
